summary:
Mauritius decriminalised same-sex conduct on 4 October 2023, when the Supreme Court struck down Section 250 of the Criminal Code of 1838 as unconstitutional, ruling that it must be read to exclude consensual acts. The provision had carried penal servitude of up to five years. Prosecutions were rare: the US State Department's 2016 country report found that sodomy references arose overwhelmingly in heterosexual divorce proceedings as an aggravating factor, although a same-sex couple was arrested in 2015 on suspicion of practising sodomy. In October 2019 a group of young people filed a constitutional challenge to Section 250, supported by the Young Queer Alliance and the Love Honor Cherish Foundation, alongside activist Abdool Ridwan Firaas Ah Seek, 29, backed by Collectif Arc-En-Ciel.

Legal gender recognition is not available in Mauritius. The Civil Status Act of 1981 and the Central Population Database form the framework under which trans Mauritians are denied recognition, according to an AfricLaw analysis of 23 August 2024. The Young Queer Alliance's July 2021 policy brief on administrative recognition of trans people argued for legal gender recognition and noted that the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders in 2019, calling on Mauritius to join countries recognising gender identity in law. Outright International's country overview, last updated 12 March 2026, records that legal gender recognition remains not possible and that progress for trans and intersex people has been 'less evident' than advances for lesbian, gay and bisexual people since the 2023 repeal.

No same-sex marriage or civil union is recognised. The Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Under the 2021 Civil Status Act, intersex newborns may be registered as 'undetermined', but nonconsensual intersex medical procedures are not banned. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Visibility carries documented risk. During the 2024 national elections, a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and other candidates used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech. Pride has been held since 2005 with counter-protesters present; in 2018 the Pride march was annulled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, and a counter-protest was organised by Javed Meetoo, an Islamic extremist under state surveillance. Earlier in 2018 a strong police force had been deployed to protect marchers, and an LGBTQ sit-in at the Caudan Waterfront followed with the Prime Minister's support. Collectif Arc-En-Ciel, founded in 2005, organised the country's first Pride and has done so for fifteen years, drawing more than 1,200 participants in 2016 when the march moved from Rose-Hill to Port Louis.

The US State Department's 2016 report documented LGBTI victims of family verbal abuse or violence reporting to local NGOs including Collectif Arc-en-Ciel and Young Queer Alliance, and recorded harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing; no later trans-specific incident is documented in this record. The 2024 AfricLaw analysis describes pervasive stigmatisation alongside the participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan, the first transgender woman in Miss Universe Mauritius 2024, and concludes that legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate despite the visibility milestone.

Access to care is uneven. According to the government, hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals, but gender-affirming care is available only in limited form, and LGBTQ people may face discrimination notably in public hospitals. In 2014 the Ministry of Health amended blood donation policy to allow men who have sex with men to donate, although anecdotally LGBTQI persons have still been prevented from donating on occasion.

Conservative attitudes remain commonplace. AfriGay reports that gay life is fairly quiet, existing mainly online, in private and at occasional parties, though resorts are welcoming and non-discriminatory and no problems with LGBTQ couples sharing hotel rooms have been recorded. LGBTQ people may face bullying in schools, while acceptance is growing particularly among the younger generation, with polls indicating Mauritius is one of Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries; a 2016 poll found 49% of Mauritians would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour. State and religious actors have also shown support: Cardinal Maurice Piat and other religious leaders condemned the anti-LGBTQ protest and called for tolerance, and the Opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights.
tangentialFactors:
Outright International's overview notes that advances since the 2023 decriminalisation have been concentrated among lesbian, gay and bisexual people, with progress for trans and intersex people 'less evident'. A traveller whose documents or presentation do not match will therefore encounter a different legal position from the one the Section 250 repeal suggests.

The 2024 election rhetoric, in which a parliamentary candidate called sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation', indicates that official-level hostility remains present in political discourse even as the courts and some state actors have moved toward protection. This sits alongside documented police protection of Pride marchers and prime-ministerial support for an LGBTQ sit-in, so state posture is not uniform.

Comparatively, polls cited in the record place Mauritius among Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries, and a 2016 poll found 49% of Mauritians would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour. These figures measure general LGBTQ attitudes, not trans-specific attitudes or trans-specific violence rates, and no trans-specific violence rate with a denominator appears in this record.
